stories.title_en: UUIDv7 doesn't have the properties you think it does

comments.author: hackingonempty
comments.text:
> If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index.
I thought the main reason UUIDv7 was created with a time component is to keep temporally related rows together in the index pages.  Randomly distributed row ids seem OK until the entire index no longer fits in RAM.

comments.author: skrebbel
comments.text:
I feel like this article way downplays the entire point of UUIDv7s, which is that it lets you sort (and store!) your data
kinda sorta
by creation time, no overlap ever. That's great for cursors, for streaming data, for twitter clones, for chat messages, for player moves, and so on and so forth. Nearly everything that's vaguely realtimey that you might like to both persist and broadcast live to other clients, and displayed in a stable & reasonable order, benefits from a property like this.
In fairness, he does mention this, but squeezes it into a single sentence near the end. But eg the fact that you can't reliably extract the precise timestamp from the UUIDv7 is a feature, not a bug. It's either that or collisions and you don't want the collisions.

stories.title_en: Docker is weird

comments.author: shykes
comments.text:
Hi, I'm the creator of Docker and came across this post. It's always fun to see other engineers think about how you designed a system. I haven't been involved in developing Docker in many years, but it's a fun trip down memory lane.
I'm happy to answer any questions you may have.

comments.author: vbezhenar
comments.text:
What made Docker unique IMO is not the container technology itself. I used chroot 20 years ago and it worked just fine. Yes, no network namespaces; no process namespaces, but I don't even think these are that important.
What made Docker unique were there things:
1. Dockerfile concept. Building images layer by layer. Caching layers. Everything in a single file. It made possible to iterate on image quickly. It made possible to implement CI builds efficiently.
2. Docker network registry concept. Putting universal images onto a server and share them with the world.
3. Momentum. A lot of software that was traditionally complicated to deploy, suddenly appeared in docker servers. I remember how fascinated I was, when I could deploy wordpress website with tiny docker-compose. And how contained it was. I could just delete every trace of it from my host. I always felt uneasy installing various things onto my host and docker just solved that uneasiness.

A few cool tricks:
`range shell python:3.12` - opens a shell image without pulling the entire image.

`range run --network none ubuntu` - network-isolated sandbox
range run ebs://snap-... -- cat /etc/os-release - opens an EBS snapshot with no EC2 instance
Another cool trick:

comments.author: martincsweiss
comments.text:
Co-author here - first paper from my postdoc accepted to NeurIPS main conference.
We built a way to sample diverse ideas in machine learning - ideas that make scientific sense, but that no existing research community is positioned to propose.
In short, the way it works is like this:
1. Take 16,068 LLM papers (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, ACL, EMNLP, 2017 to 2025) are broken into 273 "idea atoms". Every paper, and every candidate idea, becomes a set of atoms.
2. Train a Coherence Model: a 42.8M-parameter transformer trained on papers as sequences of atoms. Basically a language model whose tokens are ideas.
3. Train a Cognitive-Availability Model: a dual encoder trained on the publication histories of 39,791 researchers, which predicts where each person could plausibly go next.
4. Use those models to score sampled tuples using reciprocal rank fusion (you want ideas that go together well, but that are not cognitively available to anyone).
We tested it in a bunch of ways. One interesting one was that we took all the papers at the end of 2024, then checked which high-scoring tuples showed up in 2025 papers. It worked well - one examples is an ICLR 2025 oral, goes from rank 1,489 with coherence

Apparently agents will collude to break out of their individual sandboxes by delegating tasks to other agents that have the required permissions. This is a problem with agent fleets, because you need them to coordinate on their tasks. So you need to them to communicate.

If one of the agent decides that needs to publish the raw data, then chances are that they will collude to make that happen, even though no single agent has the permissions to achieve that goal.

comments.author: pradn
comments.text:
Frontier AIs are already smart enough to find ways to get out of sandboxes, circumvent permissions, and devise side-channels. Anthropic has shown formal verification is possible at scale. [1]
What this means is that the only hope for secure applications is security by construction, with formal methods. The race is on for constructing formally verified primitives with more and more expansive guarantees. The Anthropic/Theorem proofs show lack of memory sanitization issues. But that's just one class of problem.
Imagine a chip, a minimal boot loader, a minimal Linux, and an application library stack - all verified with high level guarantees. Then, you can plug in your application development to give you end-to-end verification guarantees. ie: no way to leak credentials at any level from the chip up to the application. No sense in your foundation being so strong if your application has easy RCEs. You need a full stack approach.
I know I'm describing a far off dream world, but it may be what's required to quell the economic "bomb" of so much dev time "wasted" in patching vulns, against actual feature dev / business value generation.

Specifications: Were hopefully correctly modeled to the Problem.
In IEEE terms:
> Verification: "Are we building the product right?"
> Validation: "Are we building the right product?")
You can write mathematically flawless code that highly efficiently solves the wrong problem.
---
While I think formal verification is the future (essential for cybersecurity), it's not a silver bullet for the other 2 items, which are way more ambiguous. I think however they can all iterate on each other and improve the project overall, but it still depends on competent steering
If you have had experiences with good approaches for verification Validation & Specification framework, do let us know about them.

comments.author: icegreentea2
comments.text:
The system in question is basically just a directed microwave emitter. It is designed to heat up the first ~0.5mm of your skin.
It's safety is basically completely a function of the operator. Since the beam will keep depositing energy (ie heating), if the beam is held on a target, it will incur more and more heating (and potentially harm).
In proper usage, safety is ensured through the combination of operator training, selection of proper settings, and induced compliance. If you have a shitty operator, risk of over exposure increases. The nature of this device means that it's not a barrier, it's a beam.
During earlier testing, they were able to induce second degree burns on a test subject due to incorrect power and duration settings.
